Research Question 2: Associations Between Cognitive Skills and Inquiry Facets
How are cognitive skills associated with specific inquiry facets, and do these associations
vary across learner profiles?
To test the role of each cognitive skill within the SDDS framework, we focus on three
key facets: (i) generating hypotheses, (ii) conducting experiments, and (iii) interpreting
results and articulating variable relations. The following hypotheses were preregistered:
H2.1 (experiment space – extent of search): Content knowledge is negatively associated
with the number of experiments (fewer, more targeted tests).
H2.2 (hypothesis space – initial hypothesis quality): Content knowledge is positively
associated with initial hypothesis quality (content knowledge provides context).
H2.3 (experiment space – control of variables): CVS is positively associated with the
proportion of valid (unconfounded) experiments (translates into practice).
H2.4 (relation space – interpreting results): Functional thinking is positively associ-
ated with relation-space outcomes (accurate variable association identification and impact
ratings).
As with RQ1, we examine whether these skill–facet links differ across learner profiles,
consistent with person-centered perspectives that such variations can inform adaptive
guidance.
Methods
Open Science
All data, R code, study materials, and the preregistration are available on the Open Science
Framework (OSF; repository: https://osf.io/qenjc; preregistration: https://osf.io/6wspv).
Deviations from the preregistration are documented in Supplementary Materials, Sect. 1.
Participants
Data were collected from 232 participants (mean age: 20.64, SD = 1.23). Gender identity
distribution was 73% female, 26% male, and 1% diverse/not specified. Most participants
(84%) were undergraduates in their third semester on average (SD = 1.82). Their fields of
study varied, with 22% in education, 15% in economics, 11% in psychology/sociology,
7% in social work, 6% in medicine, and 6% in languages. The remaining participants were
employed or seeking work (6%), in vocational training (6%), or attending school (4%).
The study targeted young adults aged 18–22, selected for their ability to complete an
extensive online study independently and for comparability with school-based samples.
Because our research questions center on individual differences in inquiry learning, we inten-
tionally sought wide variation in knowledge, skills, and dispositions to examine their influ-
ence on performance and enable informative profile analyses. Participants were required to
have at least B2-level German proficiency. Those studying natural sciences or already hold-
ing university degrees were excluded to avoid ceiling effects. Recruitment began in a south-
western German city and later expanded online across Germany and Austria. This study was
conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and national research

Measures
Predictors of Inquiry Performance: Cognitive and Dispositional Factors
Table 1 summarizes the nine instruments used to assess four cognitive factors (content
knowledge, CVS, functional thinking, general cognitive ability), four dispositional factors
(interest and self-concept in physics, personality, current motivation), and two cognitive
load factors.
To clearly distinguish CVS and functional thinking from content knowledge, none of
their test items referred to floating and sinking or to the Cartesian diver context. The CVS
tests, adapted from Schwichow et al. (2016a, b), covered physics (e.g., electricity), chemis-
try, biology, and everyday life scenarios. The functional-thinking test (Becker et al., 2019)
employed uniform-motion (kinematics) items emphasizing multi-representational reason-
ing while minimizing overlap with buoyancy or pressure content, and keeping demands
manageable for this sample.
Current motivation in the inquiry task was measured to capture task-specific disposi-
tional variance. Each instrument underwent confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to deter-
mine unidimensionality (Widaman & Revelle, 2022). Because the “interest in physics”
variable included two dimensions (theoretical discourse, hands-on activities), separate sum
scores were computed. One current motivation item (“This task is a real challenge for me.”)
was excluded after item correlations suggested participants interpreted it as referring to task
difficulty rather than personal challenge.
Dependent Variable: Inquiry Performance
Inquiry performance was assessed with seven facets aligned with the conceptualization,
investigation, and conclusion phases of inquiry in the SDDS model. Participants used a
web-based R Shiny application to explore a simplified Cartesian diver system (see Supple-
mentary Materials, Sect. 3). The application included a warm-up and an introduction to the
diver’s components, after which participants were asked to formulate an initial hypothesis
on how the diver works. Hypotheses were coded as nonspecific (no or vague statement),
intermediate (statement of effect direction), or concise (statement of direction and mecha-
nism). Table 2 shows coding examples. Coding details are provided in the preregistration.
During a 15–20 min experimentation phase, participants tested five independent vari-
ables (applied pressure, pressure point, ambient temperature, fluid density, and diver’s nut
mass), each at three possible levels, while observing six dependent variables (e.g., mean
density, buoyant force). Results were presented as animations (diver’s behavior) and numer-
ical tables for both conditions (see Fig. 2 for a screenshot of the setup). Pressure had the

underlying forces. Facets 5–7 used structured response formats and were scored according
to correctness, as responses were closed and did not require qualitative coding. These facets
encompass all SDDS spaces. The variable space is reflected in identifying independent and
dependent variables, while the whole hypothesis space is engaged in formulating initial
hypotheses. The experiment space is represented in conducting experiments. The final four
facets (4–7) correspond to the relation space, assessing how well learners synthesized vari-
able relations and refined their hypotheses based on experimental results. These outcome
measures capture the final state of the hypothesis space, indicating the extent to which learn-
ers integrated their findings. The seven facets were combined into a single factor score (see

evaluation of variable impact.

Procedure
Participants completed a six-session online procedure (Fig. 3) hosted on the Gorilla Experi-
ment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020). Session 1 (T1) included pre-tests on cognitive
skills (content knowledge, CVS, functional thinking). Session 2 (T2) assessed demograph-
ics, dispositional factors (interest, self-concept in physics, personality), and general cogni-
tive ability.
Participants were then randomly assigned to one of six learning-sequence conditions
(T3–T5) or to an untrained control group. Each learning session provided direct instruc-
tion on one target skill (content knowledge, CVS, or functional thinking) followed by a
post-test. They did not include inquiry tasks nor did they address Cartesian-diver concepts.
Randomization controlled for potential order effects. The final session (T6) comprised the
Cartesian diver inquiry task. Afterward, participants submitted payment information and
verified their age.
On average, the study took about 4.25 h. Analyses in this paper used T6 inquiry-task
outcomes, T2 covariates, and the most recent skill assessments (T3–T5 for trained partici-
pants, T1 for untrained controls) prior to the inquiry task. Data from the learning sessions
themselves were not analyzed for the present research questions.
Statistical Approaches
Missing Data and Data Quality
Missing data were minimal because participants were required to respond to most items,
except in the Cartesian diver application, resulting in < 5% missingness for that task. No
discernible pattern emerged. To ensure data quality, responses were evaluated for care-
less responding (e.g., implausible durations, inconsistent pre–post scores, failed attention
checks). Skill assessments and the 60-item personality inventory were coded as missing
where multiple indicators suggested inattentive responses. This affected six skill sum scores.
For the personality data, slightly less than 10% failed checks. All missing data were imputed
using multiple imputation (D. B. Rubin, 2018), resulting in a final dataset with no missing
values. Imputation at the sum score level offered stable solutions and yielded distributions
nearly identical to the raw data.

Modeling
All overall effects were examined via regression for consistency in reporting and interpreta-
tion. To address RQ1 (predictors of inquiry performance), a hierarchical multiple regres-
sion was used, entering variables in three blocks (cognitive factors, dispositional factors,
and cognitive load). Differential effects were then assessed through latent profile analy-
sis (LPA) to identify distinct learner profiles. The LPA summarized multivariate learner
states before and during inquiry and was used to support profile-based moderation analyses.
Model selection followed Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and integrated complete
likelihood (ICL), with final profiles evaluated for interpretability and theoretical coherence.
Profile membership probabilities were visually examined, and bootstrapping checked esti-
mate reliability.
RQ2 (associations between skills and inquiry facets) used regression models tailored to
the dependent variable (linear or nonlinear). To determine whether these associations varied
across the learner profiles found in RQ1, models were refitted for each subgroup, comparing
overall and subgroup effects descriptively. Identifying diverging skill-facet associations can
inform the design of adaptive guidance. All regression models were checked for linearity,
homogeneity of variance, collinearity (VIF > 3), normality of residuals, and outlier lever-
age. When outliers were identified, a robust Mahalanobis distance approach (Leys et al.,
2018) was used to exclude them, followed by an impact assessment. Predictor variables and
inquiry performance factor scores were z-standardized before modeling. As preregistered,
no p-value adjustments were made, since each hypothesis was tested individually (Rubin,
2021).
Results
RQ1: Effects of Cognitive and Dispositional Predictors on Inquiry Performance
To assess how cognitive and dispositional factors influenced performance in the Cartesian
diver inquiry task, hierarchical multiple regression analyses were performed. The models,
summarized in Fig. 4, introduced predictors in three successive blocks. The first model
(block 1, blue) included post-test scores of content knowledge, CVS, functional thinking,
and general cognitive ability, each of which significantly contributed to performance. This
model explained approximately 49% of the variance in inquiry task scores. In the second
model (block 2, green), dispositional variables (interest in physics, self-concept in physics,
the six personality dimensions, and current motivation) were added. A more positive phys-
ics self-concept was associated with better performance, although including dispositional
measures did not increase the model’s overall explanatory power. The final model (block 3,
orange) added intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load, revealing a significant negative effect
of extraneous load on inquiry performance and producing an additional 5% increase in
explained variance. All model coefficients are available in Supplementary Materials, Sect.
5.1. Results for sociodemographic variables such as age, gender, language, and occupation
are omitted because their effects were negligible and variance was low. A sensitivity analy-
sis based on elastic net regularization indicated that the findings remained stable (Supple-
mentary Materials, Sect. 5.2).

RQ2: Evaluating the Impact of Individual Skills on Different Inquiry Facets
Building on RQ1, we examined how individual cognitive skills affected specific inquiry
facets. For each preregistered hypothesis, multiple regression models included the predic-
tors most influential in overall performance (content knowledge, CVS, functional thinking,
general cognitive ability, self-concept, and extraneous load). To assess profile differences,
the same models were re-estimated for each LPA subgroup. To avoid circularity, we refitted
the profile solution without inquiry-performance scores, as some of the examined inquiry
facets entered overall inquiry performance scores. 89% of participants retained their origi-
nal classification, indicating profiling consistency.
The first analysis investigated how content knowledge influences the number of experi-
ments conducted (H2.1). It was hypothesized that individuals with greater content knowl-
edge would engage in fewer, more targeted experiments as a strategic approach to hypothesis
testing. The left panel of Fig. 6 illustrates this association using a scatterplot of content
knowledge against the number of experiments performed. Because the association appeared
non-linear, a polynomial regression analysis (up to fifth order) was conducted, and a second-
order regression model was chosen based on its lowest AIC value and parsimony. Gen-
eral cognitive ability also showed a quadratic association with the number of experiments,
whereas other covariates were included with linear terms only. To address potential outliers,
data from two participants who performed more than 60 experiments were excluded, as
those values suggested a lack of earnest effort or technical artifacts. In the refined analysis,
neither the linear component (β = 0.23, p =.760) nor the quadratic component (β = −0.79,
p =.105) of content knowledge was significant, while the quadratic component of general
cognitive ability (β = −1.10, p =.038) was significant. Participants with lower general cogni-
tive ability conducted fewer experiments, while those with higher ability initially conducted
more. However, this effect reversed at approximately half a standard deviation above the
mean, where further increases in cognitive ability were associated with conducting fewer
experiments. Self-concept also showed a negative linear effect (β = −1.40, p =.011), indi-
cating that higher self-concept was associated with conducting fewer experiments. At the
profile level, using only linear components, the model explained variance only for the opti-

Discussion
This study examined which factors shape simulation-based inquiry performance in physics.
Two principal questions guided our investigation: first, which cognitive, dispositional, and
load factors predict inquiry performance across learner profiles; second, how these factors
link to specific inquiry facets. The results show that cognitive factors play a dominant role
in driving performance, though their exact impact depends on learners’ skill levels and
the inquiry facet. The following discussion situates these findings within the context of
prior research and the SDDS framework, and highlights their implications for increasing the
effectiveness of inquiry-based learning.
RQ1: Crucial Skills for Inquiry Performance
Our findings indicate that four cognitive factors - content knowledge, CVS, functional
thinking, and general cognitive ability - explain around half of the variance in performance
on the Cartesian diver task. Dispositional factors and cognitive load added little explana-
tory power, apart from extraneous cognitive load. This result aligns with hypothesis H1.1
and prior work emphasizing the centrality of cognitive skills in inquiry performance among
school-aged students (Nehring et al., 2015). Although variables such as interest and self-
concept can influence engagement and the effective use of cognitive skills (Nehring et al.,
2015; Omarchevska et al., 2023), their impact here was limited. One possible explanation is
that the inclusion of a broader set of cognitive variables in our analysis may have captured
variance that would otherwise be attributed to dispositional factors. For example, if interest
contributes to inquiry performance primarily through its association with content knowl-
edge or other cognitive skills, its independent effect may no longer be detectable. This does
not necessarily imply that dispositional factors are unimportant; rather, their role may be
more pronounced in the long-term development of cognitive skills rather than in their appli-
cation to specific tasks. In naturalistic settings that afford sustained engagement over weeks,
dispositional effects may be stronger, because they can influence learning outcomes through
engagement and effects on metacognition (Kubsch et al., 2023). Regardless of whether this
pattern reflects the scope of our modeling or characteristics of our sample, the data suggest
that aligning learners’ proficiency in a few key cognitive factors with task demands can
substantially enhance inquiry efficiency.
Performance profiles further showed that cognitive skills were highly interrelated, con-
sistent with H1.2.1–H1.2.3, while dispositional attributes varied only minimally between
profiles. These findings are consistent with earlier work that has demonstrated substantial
correlations between content knowledge and CVS (Nehring & Schwichow, 2020; Oster-
haus et al., 2017; Schwichow et al., 2020) and between content knowledge and functional
thinking (Becker et al., 2019; Rittle-Johnson et al., 2015). The smaller but still meaningful
correlation between CVS and functional thinking suggests that deficits in one skill often
accompany deficits in others, indicating potential value in integrative rather than purely
task-embedded guidance. Providing numerous prompts or extensive information for each

skill simultaneously risks cognitive overload (Eckhardt et al., 2013), especially for learners
with low foundational competence. Structuring tasks around smaller goals, such as guiding
learners to apply CVS strategies while offering pre-defined hypotheses, may yield incre-
mental gains.
Extraneous cognitive load emerged as another significant predictor. Its linear negative
effect underscores the interplay between learner characteristics and task demands, consis-
tent with prior findings (Nehring et al., 2015). However, the profile analysis revealed that
reported extraneous load within the same group could be highly variable. Some participants
who appeared overwhelmed still reported relatively low extraneous load, suggesting that
subjective load ratings may not always match actual task demands. In the present digital
task, such variability may also have reflected how learners coordinated the graphical inter-
face, visual and tabular outputs, and note-taking options. This interpretation is consistent
with Joo et al. (2021), who emphasize that visual representations and scaffolds in multi-
representational learning need to be carefully adapted to learner progress. The variability
within groups is consistent with the potential value of adaptive guidance in digital simula-
tions that can respond to real-time learner progress. Designing tasks with manageable goals
based on learner proficiency could help maintain an optimal challenge level, while carefully
calibrated in-task support can accommodate different cognitive needs within proficiency
groups.
Overall, these results underscore the central role of cognitive factors in inquiry learning
while emphasizing the importance of balancing general task design, scaffolded structures,
and adaptive guidance to serve learners across a wide skill range. Uniformly offering a
single inquiry task with the same supports might lead to cognitive overload for those with
weaker foundational skills and insufficient challenge for those with stronger skills. This
outcome is consistent with the SDDS model’s portrayal of inquiry as a cyclical process that
coordinates multiple correlated skills. Instructional methods may therefore integrate diverse
types of scaffolding, including task structuring, goal-setting, and flexible on-demand guid-
ance, in order to align with learners’ general proficiency levels and address specific skill
deficits. The following section discusses the associations between skills and specific inquiry
facets, which can inform effective in-task guidance for specific activities.
RQ2: Cognitive Skills and Individual Inquiry Facets
The second research question examined how cognitive skills influence specific inquiry
facets. Findings indicate that content knowledge, CVS, and functional thinking each play
a significant role, aligning with the SDDS framework. CVS skill was closely linked to
conducting valid experiments, as stated in H2.3, reinforcing the idea that higher CVS pro-
ficiency translates into more accurate experimental behavior. Importantly, these findings
reaffirm that CVS is not a skill automatically mastered with age but must be actively taught
(Schwichow et al. 2016a, b). Even within our predominantly university-level sample, about
half of the participants exhibited deficits in CVS, consistent with prior research suggest-
ing that a substantial portion of young adults fail to master this skill (Schwichow et al.,
2020). These findings are consistent with the value of incorporating guidance into inquiry
tasks, particularly in non-specialist STEM classrooms, to support learners lacking CVS
proficiency.

Functional thinking likewise emerged as an important complement to content knowl-
edge and CVS. It consistently predicted task performance (in line with H2.4), particularly
for facets involving interpretation of variable associations, which the SDDS framework
conceptualizes as operations within the relation space. Tasks such as naming key variable
associations or assessing variable impacts on the Cartesian diver system emphasize how
functional thinking enables learners to move flexibly between representations and reason
about variable relations. However, functional thinking’s benefits appear partly contingent
on foundational skills such as CVS, which remains the strongest overall predictor of inquiry
performance. This interplay aligns with prior research showing that functional thinking sup-
ports learning gains and deeper conceptual understanding (Becker et al., 2020) and benefits
from mutual reinforcement with experimentation in uncovering covariance patterns (Digel
et al., 2023; Koerber et al., 2005; Lichti & Roth, 2018).
Content knowledge demonstrated a more nuanced influence on individual inquiry facets.
It did not predict the total number of experiments performed, contrary to the hypothesis
that it would shape either exploratory or targeted experimental approaches (H2.1). Instead,
general cognitive ability and self-concept exerted modest effects on experimental behavior,
with data suggesting that participants at lower skill levels were sometimes overwhelmed,
while those at higher skill levels seemed to plateau or slightly reduce the number of experi-
ments they performed.
Content knowledge also exhibited limited predictive power for initial hypothesis qual-
ity in the lower-to-middle skill range, where general factors like self-concept and extrane-
ous cognitive load were more informative. However, for higher-skilled participants, content
knowledge tentatively showed stronger effects, aligning with prior findings that content
knowledge is essential for hypothesis formation (Alexander & Judy, 1988; Hattie & Dono-
ghue, 2016; Hulshof & de Jong, 2006; Lazonder et al., 2008; Sandoval & Reiser, 2004;
Schneider & Preckel, 2017). Only learners with some content knowledge can base their
hypotheses on it. Overall, hypothesis H2.2 is only partially supported. Notably, our findings
suggest that inquiry skills such as CVS are also critical; without them, learners struggle to
effectively use their content knowledge to formulate and test hypotheses.
While the lower-than-expected effect of content knowledge on initial hypothesis qual-
ity could also be explained by the far-transfer nature of the inquiry task and by the fact
that only the initial hypothesis was considered, these results highlight the importance of
comprehensively modeling inquiry skills. The strong bivariate association between content
knowledge and initial hypothesis quality alone suggests that hypothesis generation aid may
focus on providing domain information. However, our profile analysis indicates that such
aid would likely be ineffective for learners with lower inquiry skills like CVS. Ensuring that
learners have the necessary inquiry skills (and the belief that they do) to translate domain
information into actionable hypotheses appears important when designing support. In light
of these findings, the extended SDDS framework (van Joolingen & de Jong, 1997) offers a
useful tool for informing the design of guidance by making explicit the cognitive operations
involved in inquiry. For example, the relation space within the hypothesis space provides
a detailed description of the search operations concerning variable associations, including
identifying relations, recognizing their absence, and defining the boundary conditions of
these associations. Such explicit representations may enable targeted guidance. If a learner
struggles to interpret variable associations based on experimental results, and our findings
indicate that functional thinking is the predominant skill required, guidance can focus on

conditions for observed relations. These approaches align the guidance with the operations
outlined in the relation space, supporting learners in both immediate challenges and broader

informing the design of flexible and context-sensitive guidance. By making cognitive opera-

with the inherent complexity of inquiry.
Implications for Inquiry Research
Our findings carry several implications for inquiry learning research. First, our results
highlight the impact of analytical choices on outcomes, specifically how comprehensively
inquiry skills are modeled and whether sample-wide or subgroup-focused approaches are
used. This sensitivity is illustrated by the varying results concerning content knowledge’s
role in hypothesis generation. In a simple regression model, content knowledge showed a
strong association with hypothesis quality. However, this association disappeared in a mul-
tiple regression model and was more pronounced among higher-skilled participants than
lower-skilled ones. Each analytical approach would have led to different implications for
guidance design, such as whether providing domain-specific content knowledge is an effec-
tive strategy for facilitating hypothesis generation. Our findings emphasize the importance
of triangulating sample-wide and subgroup-focused approaches to capture the complexity
of inquiry processes and better tailor interventions to learner needs (Omarchevska et al.,
2023).
Second, our findings emphasize the need for comprehensive inquiry skill models that
incorporate not only content knowledge and process skills like CVS but also less-studied
skills such as functional thinking (or some other form of representational competence and
relational reasoning). Research has shown that these skills are important predictors of sci-
entific reasoning (Koerber & Osterhaus, 2019) and learning gains (Schlatter et al., 2020) in
children. Additionally, inquiry models typically conceptualize more than content knowledge
and CVS as required skills (Pedaste et al., 2015), yet they are seldom modeled concur-
rently in studies. Incorporating them into a unified framework can illuminate how various
cognitive skills operate together to drive inquiry performance. This aligns with our finding
that functional thinking relies on foundational skills such as CVS for effective data inter-
pretation, while content knowledge provides the domain-specific context for forming and
testing hypotheses. Accounting for these interdependent skills reveals deeper insights into
the inquiry process and permits the development of more precisely targeted instructional
strategies.
Limitations
This study offers insights into the interplay of inquiry skills through a far-transfer simula-
tion-based inquiry task conducted with a non-school sample of young adults in the physics
context of floating and sinking. While the findings largely align with existing theory and
prior research, several considerations regarding their generalization are warranted.

First, the specificity of the task and sample likely shaped some results. For instance, the
lower observed effects of content knowledge may reflect the far-transfer nature of the task
and its focus on initial hypotheses. Similarly, the influence of functional thinking on inquiry
performance may depend on the design of the task’s data representations and the inherent
complexity of the system being investigated. The results related to CVS may also have been
affected by ceiling effects, as the majority of participants were university students.
Second, the use of a data-driven LPA to explore differential effects is another factor to
consider. While this approach offers valuable insights into the variability of skill-perfor-
mance associations, the specific group characteristics identified in this study may not repli-
cate across other contexts or populations.
In summary, the results should be interpreted within the context of the task design, sam-
ple characteristics, and analytic approach. While broader conclusions, such as the predomi-
nance of cognitive over dispositional factors in inquiry performance, appear robust, subtler
findings, such as the relative predictive strength of individual skills, may vary meaningfully
in other contexts. Future research should further investigate how variations in context and
participant populations influence the interplay of cognitive skills and whether these differ-
ences call for alternative instructional designs.
Conclusion
This study provides a comprehensive view of how content knowledge, CVS, and functional
thinking jointly influence simulation-based inquiry learning within a physics context. The
findings highlight these skills’ central role and show that each skill’s effect can vary accord-
ing to learners’ proficiency levels.
The results support the conclusion that CVS and functional thinking are vital for design-
ing valid experiments and identifying variable relations, consistent with the SDDS frame-
work. Neither skill develops automatically through maturation, making explicit instruction
necessary, even among university students. Functional thinking, which facilitates data inter-
pretation and relational reasoning, also emerged as a robust predictor of overall inquiry per-
formance, complementing the traditional focus on content knowledge and CVS in inquiry
learning. These findings reinforce the need for multifaceted modeling of cognitive skills so
that guidance design can precisely target the facets where learners most need support.
Finally, our results highlight the importance of analytical choices in inquiry research.
Sample-wide versus subgroup-specific analyses revealed differential effects, illustrating the
value of comprehensive skill modeling to capture nuanced learner profiles.
In summary, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of how individual skills
shape inquiry performance and offers actionable insights for designing inquiry-based learn-
ing environments. By aligning guidance strategies with learners’ skills and focusing on
adequate learning goals, educators can better support students in developing the critical
cognitive skills necessary for successful inquiry learning.

Developing pre‑service teachers’ TPACK for programming
simulations
Niklas Karlsen1 · Siv Aalbergsjø1
Received: 23 May 2024 / Accepted: 25 June 2026
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
Modeling using simulations is a promising approach for integrating programming into sci-
ence education. In this paper we use the technological pedagogical and content knowledge
(TPACK) framework developed by Mishra and Koehler (2006) to examine and develop
pre-service teachers’ (PSTs’) knowledge of integrating computational thinking into science
education in the context of programming simulations in Scratch. We have used design-
based research to develop a learning sequence for PSTs concerning this topic. Through
two iterations we explored how the learning sequence contributed to developing PSTs’
TPACK. We investigated PSTs’ learning processes when they designed lesson plans for
teaching programming of simulations in science education aimed at the lower secondary
level. Our results suggest that PSTs’ TPACK developed when creating lesson plans fitted to
simulations created during the learning sequence. In addition, we found that PSTs shifted
their focus from the programming content to the science content when we made the inquiry
and modeling elements more explicit during the programming. Based on this, we propose
design principles for developing PSTs’ TPACK related to the programming of simulations
of science phenomena.
Keywords Science teacher education · Programming · Modeling and simulation · TPACK
Introduction
Computational thinking (CT) is an important scientific practice. It relates to both mod-
eling and simulation and computational problem solving using programming (Weintrop
et al., 2016). Programming concerns reading, running, and modifying computer code (Peel
et al., 2021). Researchers have demonstrated the promise of programming simulations as
an approach for teaching pre-service teachers (PSTs) how to integrate CT into science edu-
cation (Adler & Kim, 2018; Rachmatullah & Wiebe, 2023; Vasconcelos & Kim, 2020b,
2022). However, other researchers examining how PSTs understand CT and its integration
into science lessons with simulations, have found PSTs’ understanding of CT to be limited

(Kale et al., 2023; Killen et al., 2023; Moon et al., 2023). Dong et al. (2024) suggest that
a shortcoming of such CT courses for PSTs is that they often focus on theoretical learning
rather than practical applications which are more readily transferrable to classroom prac-
tice. Also, recent reviews show there are relatively few studies that focus on CT-science
integration and CT teaching approaches for PSTs, which strengthens the need for more
research on how to teach pedagogical practices for CT to PSTs (Ottenbreit-Leftwich et al.,
2021; Sundtjønn et al., 2024; Yun & Crippen, 2024).
Our work is related to this issue and positions itself as design-based research (DBR).
DBR aims to develop theoretical understanding through the design of pedagogical inter-
ventions (Wang & Hannafin, 2005). Accordingly, we have designed a learning sequence
for PSTs on programmable simulations in science education. Our aim was to explore how
PSTs can be prepared to integrate programming into science education. A preliminary
study was completed around 2020 and further adapted and developed the following years
(Aalbergsjø, 2022; Aalbergsjø & Karlsen, 2023; Karlsen & Aalbergsjø, 2023, 2024). The
current article reports the result of this work in the form of design principles for designing
such learning sequences.
The main purpose of this article is to discuss the design process and how it led to the
suggested design principles. Our design revisions were informed by our analyses of how
PSTs’ knowledge developed through the learning sequence. A well established framework
for teachers’ technological pedagogical content knowledge is the technological pedagogi-
cal and content knowledge (TPACK) framework developed by Mishra and Koehler (2006).
We have used TPACK to conceptualize PSTs’ knowledge of how to integrate CT in science
education using an adaptation of TPACK for the context of programming in science educa-
tion developed by Karlsen et al. (2025).
In this article we address the following research questions:
RQ1: Which components of TPACK are used by the PSTs in the learning sequence?
RQ2: Which components of the PSTs’ self-reported TPACK changed during the learn-
ing sequence?
RQ3: Which paths for TPACK development do the PSTs follow during the learning
sequence?
Next, we describe our theoretical framework, context and methodological approach. Then
a design narrative (Hoadley, 2002) is used to describe how our design was developed
through two iterations. We include results from the field testing of each prototype design
to strengthen the design narrative. Finally, we discuss the results and present our proposed
design principles as implications of our work.
Theoretical background
To examine how to develop PSTs’ knowledge about the use of programming in science
education, we have chosen TPACK (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) as a lens for the PSTs’
knowledge development. Mishra and Koehler (2006) suggest that TPACK can be useful
both as an analytical tool when examining teaching with technology, and as a design
tool when working to develop PSTs’ knowledge about the use of technology in teach-
ing. According to the TPACK framework, knowledge about technology (TK), pedagogy
(PK) and subject content (CK) and the relation between these three knowledge areas,

text:
Developing pre‑service teachers’ TPACK for programming…
are central for teaching with technology. We consider programming as the technology
(TK), the use of computer simulations in science as technological content knowledge
(TCK) and how to teach the scientific practices of modeling in science as pedagogi-
cal content knowledge (PCK). In addition, TPACK is highly contextualized knowledge
(Petko et al., 2025). This reflects the situated nature of TPACK and how it develops.
However, context in TPACK can also be conceptualized as PSTs’ contextual knowledge
(XK), such as knowledge about pupils, school context and curriculum.
CT can be conceptualized as either practices similar to those performed by computer
scientists when programming (Wing, 2006), or as computational practices employed in
science (Peel et al., 2021; Weintrop et al., 2016). In this article we use the first meaning
in relation to TK, and in the second meaning related to TCK. To clarify what we mean
by a simulation we distinguish between animations and simulations by positing that
simulations are based on a model of a natural-science phenomenon where the param-
eters of the model can be modified, while animations focus on the visual representa-
tion of the phenomenon, not the underlying mechanics of the model. An explication
of how we conceptualize the different TPACK components is given in Table 1. As the
study is situated on campus and not in a relevant school context for the PSTs, XK is not
addressed.
Koehler et al. (2014) describe three paths to develop TPACK, either by 1) first devel-
oping PCK and then adding TK, 2) developing TPK and later combining it with CK
or 3) developing both PCK and TPACK simultaneously. The three paths are illustrated
in Fig. 1. In Path 1, PSTs develop TK and then integrate it with their previous PCK to
develop TPACK. Path 2 is not expected to be salient in a science education course since
the content is in focus. Path 3 would bring about development of both PSTs’ PCK and
TPACK by engaging their PK, CK and TK simultaneously to develop PCK and TPACK.
An example of Path 3 could be the learning-by-design approach suggested by Koe-
hler and Mishra (2006), where PSTs develop TPACK by designing learning materials.
This requires the PSTs to navigate their knowledge about technology, pedagogy, and
content simultaneously. However, since developing both PCK and TPACK simultane-
ously can be cognitively taxing (Koehler et al., 2014), there is a need to scaffold TPACK
development. This may even apply for experienced teachers who are unfamiliar with
using programming in science contexts.

Approaches such as use-modify-create (UMC) (Lee et al., 2011) or PRIMM (Sent-
ance et al., 2019) could potentially function as scaffolding to reduce the cognitive load
by supporting the development of PSTs’ TK and TCK before these need to be integrated
with PCK into TPACK. UMC has shown promise as an approach to learn programming in
STEM contexts (Houchins et al., 2021; Jocius et al., 2021), and Lee et al. (2011) showed
how UMC can be used to develop programming and CT skills through modeling and simu-
lation. Research also suggest that these approaches can support pupils learning about pro-
gramming and science content simultaneously (Franklin et al., 2020; Lytle et al., 2019).
While UMC emphasizes CT, PRIMM emphasizes programming by requiring the students
to first predict (P) what a code will do, before running (R) and investigating (I) the code
more closely, and then modifying (M) and making (M) their own code.
Methodology
Design‑based research
DBR aims to improve educational practice by pragmatically refining theory and practice
in concert through research in authentic settings (Wang & Hannafin, 2005). The prag-
matic approach is iterative and flexible, and we used mixed methods to understand how the
design supports learning. The qualitative data were collected during the programming ses-
sions, while the quantitative data were collected before and after the learning sequence as a
single group pre-post test design (Marsden & Torgerson, 2012).
Analyses of the data were used to assess and revise our design (cf. Juuti & Lavonen,
2006; McKenney & Reeves, 2018). Reflections on the results from each iteration fed into
the design revisions between trial runs, see Fig. 2. To make the process more purposeful,
we used the idea of Juuti and Lavonen (2006) to set specific goals to assess whether our Developing pre‑service teachers’ TPACK for programming…

design was feasible and determine changes between iterations. The outcome of the process
is expressed as design principles which are research-based suggestions for how to improve
practice.
This article reports from the “prototype development” stage of a learning sequence,
which involves field testing and micro evaluation of the local viability of our prototype
(McKenney & Reeves, 2018) after two iterations. The prototyping and testing were done
in collaboration with a teacher educator (second author) who taught the learning sequence.
Some of our results have previously been reported elsewhere (Aalbergsjø & Karlsen, 2023;
Karlsen & Aalbergsjø, 2023, 2024).
Context and participants
The research was done in a teacher education program at a Norwegian university in a sci-
ence education course at the master’s level, where one of the topics was simulations and
programming. The learning sequence consisted of four sessions where the PSTs first used
simulations created by the researcher and teacher educator, and then were given the task
of developing and presenting their own simulations with a corresponding lesson plan that
could be used in school science. The participants are presented in Table 2, and a total of 52
PSTs participated in the two iterations, 22 in the first prototype and 30 in the second pro-
totype. There was a large proportion of female PSTs (72%), with approximately the same
number of PSTs targeting teaching at the primary and lower secondary levels.
Data collection methods
We collected data before and after the learning sequence using a questionnaire (pre-post
tests) and video- and sound recordings of the PSTs while they were programming the sim-
ulations and presenting their own simulations and teaching plans. We also collected the
PSTs’ computer code in Scratch and presentations, and interviewed four of the PSTs after
the learning sequences. The interviews were semi-structured and asked questions related to
the PSTs experiences with and opinions about the use of programming in science educa-
tion. Before and after each iteration, PSTs answered the questionnaire.
The students worked first in pairs and then in groups of up to five PSTs. During each
session two groups were video recorded, and two groups were sound recorded. The video
camera was situated behind the PSTs to capture their interactions with the computer screen
and each other. Approximately ten hours of video and eleven hours of sound were recorded

and artifacts from five groups were collected in prototype 1. In Prototype 2, seven hours of
video and six hours of sound were recorded, and artifacts from six groups.
We used an early version of the TPACK-questionnaire developed by Karlsen et al.
(2025) as a pre-post measure of the PSTs’ self-reported knowledge. The questionnaire was
previously used by Karlsen et al. (2024) to survey the TPACK of Norwegian PSTs who
studied science education. Some example items are, TK: “I can use computational think-
ing when writing computer code”, PCK: “I have knowledge about scientific practices”,
TPACK: “I know how to use programming in science to help pupils understand scientific
concepts and phenomena.”
The items are scored on a 5-pt Likert scale from disagree strongly (1) to agree strongly
(5) and measure the three knowledge domains of TK, PCK and TPACK, and as such do not
measure all the TPACK components. We consider however that these are the most relevant
for our design in light of the three theoretical paths for developing TPACK proposed by
Koehler et al. (2014). Even though self-report data often is understood as a measure of
self-efficacy (Krauskopf & Forssell, 2018; Scherer et al., 2017), some research suggest that
“self-reported estimates of learning” can be used as a “measure of achievement” (Gonyea,
2005, p. 80–81), which gives support to the use of questionnaire data from pre-post tests as
a measure of knowledge change.
Data analysis methods
The purpose of the data analysis was to tentatively get an understanding of PSTs’ TPACK
development in order to use this understanding to support the design revision process. Both
the video- and sound recordings and interviews were analyzed qualitatively to assess the
PSTs’ learning processes during the learning sequence. The questionnaire data was ana-
lyzed quantitatively to get a tentative measure of the PSTs’ change in knowledge, as sug-
gested by Jacobsen and McKenney (2023); in addition, it was used to explore possible
TPACK development paths.
Qualitative analyses
Video and sound recordings, interview data, and the video of and artifacts from PSTs’
presentations were analyzed qualitatively to gain insight into which components of TPACK
the PSTs used during the learning sequence and to support our quantitative analyses of
PSTs’ change in TPACK. The first author created content listings of all the video and
sound recordings, and some parts were expanded with minimal transcriptions (Jordan &
Henderson, 1995). The purpose of the content listings was to create an overview of what
the PSTs were working on and talking about, and the content listings were then used for
further analysis. The audio recordings of the interviews were transcribed verbatim. For the
purpose of analyzing the presentations, the first author transcribed all these, including pic-
tures, tables and informative layout (such as arrows etc.).
Directed content analysis (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005) was used to analyze the content
listings and transcriptions in NVivo using Table 1 as the analytical framework using
all seven TPACK knowledge domains. Parts of the same material were coded by both
authors. Agreement was then reached on how to interpret the codes through discus-
sions. The complete transcribed material was then analyzed by the second author. The
data was coded as TK when the PSTs were either working on Scratch code or discuss-
ing or describing code without explicitly addressing the science content or pedagogical

text:
N. Karlsen, S. Aalbergsjø
aspects of the program. When they were discussing or describing the science content
without addressing the computer model or pedagogical aspects, this was coded as CK.
PK without science or programming was not identified in the material. TPK was coded
when the PSTs were discussing or describing how to accommodate for learning with
programming, without connecting it to the science content. TCK was coded when the
PSTs were discussing or describing the role of programming and computer models
in science in general or in relation to the content, without referring to teaching and
pedagogy. PCK was used when the PSTs were discussing teaching methods for science
content such as inquiry-based teaching and the use of models for teaching science con-
tent. And TPACK was coded when the students were discussing or describing how to
promote pupil’s learning in science using programming of simulations.
After testing Prototype 1, results from the analysis of video and sound recordings,
interviews, and the presentations were used to revise the prototype learning sequence.
After testing the revised Prototype 2, a more targeted analysis was performed, where
only content analysis of content listings from video- and sound recordings was made.
Quantitative analyses
We used quantitative analyses to explore the changes in the PSTs’ TPACK components
and the paths for developing TPACK, since these alternative paths provide important
clues to interpreting the functioning of our design. We first used simple difference
scores and statistical tests for the pre-post scores to get a first-order estimate of the
change in TPACK. The significance threshold (α) was set to 0.05, even though we did
not adhere strictly to this threshold (Cohen, 1990; Wasserstein et al., 2019). The ques-
tionnaire data show adequate reliabilities between 0.7 and 0.9 calculated with Cron-
bach’s alpha for the different TPACK elements in the individual pre and post datasets.
PSTs’ individual change in self-reported TPACK were then analyzed using fixed
effects (Allison, 2009) to determine whether the PSTs’ TPACK development was
affected by the prototype and their change in TK and PCK. One of the advantages
of fixed effects is that it controls for differences between the participants, such as
prior experiences with programming or maturation rates. Fixed effects are equivalent
to using first difference regression since we use only two time points. The value for
the vertical intercept of the regression model can therefore be interpreted as an indi-
vidual’s average change in TPACK when there is no change in TK or PCK. In addi-
tion to fixed effects, we examined within-between (hybrid) models, since these give
more information and fixed effects (i.e., within effects) is already incorporated into the
within-between model (Allison, 2009; Bell et al., 2019). The assumptions for doing
regression analysis were checked, such as normally distributed errors and linear rela-
tionships between variables. There were no missing data in the individual items.
We used R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023) for our analyses. The regression
analyses were done with the R package PLM version 2.6-3 (Croissant & Millo, 2008),
while the within-between model was examined with nlme version 3.1-163 (Pinheiro
et al., 2023). The average scores for TK, PCK and TPACK used in the regression anal-
yses were calculated using the psych package version 2.3.12 (Revelle, 2023). Statisti-
cal tests to compare differences were made with the R package WRS2 version 1.1-5
(Mair & Wilcox, 2020).

Design narrative and results
In this section we use a design narrative (Hoadley, 2002) to describe how our design
evolved. For each prototype in turn, we first present the problem description and design,
before we present the results of the analysis of that prototype. The process of designing
each prototype began with explicating the problems that we wanted to solve. We then cre-
ated goals that the design should achieve, constructed the initial prototype and tested it.
Based on the results of the analyses and our experiences from the testing of the first proto-
type, the goals were adjusted and the design revised. After the second prototype was field
tested, new analyses were conducted and abductive reasoning used to formulate our design
principles. Table 3 provides an overview of the design of each prototype and changes made
between Prototype 1 and 2 to support the reading of the design narrative.
Prototype 1
Initial problem description
A review of the literature showed that the integration of programming in science teacher
education is receiving increasing attention among researchers (e.g., Aalbergsjø, 2022; But-
ler & Leahy, 2021; Pewkam & Chamrat, 2022; Timur et al., 2021; Vasconcelos & Kim,
2020b). While previous research indicate that many PSTs find programming motivating
(Adler & Kim, 2018; Ortiz et al., 2015; Timur et al., 2021), many PSTs also seem to lack
the confidence to integrate it with their own teaching (Aalbergsjø, 2022; Margulieux &
Yadav, 2021; Rachmatullah & Wiebe, 2023). A possible explanation is that many PSTs
find programming challenging (Aalbergsjø, 2022; Kale et al., 2023), perhaps since they
have little previous experience.
Evidence was found by Aalbergsjø (2022) that TPACK development could be pro-
moted by letting the PSTs develop teaching plans for pupils incorporating programming
in science. However, developing both PCK and TPACK simultaneously can be cognitively

text:
N. Karlsen, S. Aalbergsjø
taxing (Aalbergsjø, 2022; Koehler et al., 2014). Thus, we concluded that part of the prob-
lem that needs to be solved is how to develop PSTs’ TK and simultaneously support them
in integrating this TK with their PCK to develop their knowledge of how to apply program-
ming in science education (i.e. TPACK).
Based on the above, we wanted the design to support the following goals:
1. PSTs should develop their TPACK related to programming simulations in science.
2. PSTs should develop their TK related to programming, but programming should also
be used to support the learning of science to help PSTs connect TK to PCK.
3. PSTs should develop CK and TCK related to scientific practices and simulations.
Initial design
We found few examples in the literature on the use of programming to explore simula-
tions with PSTs. However, the work by Vasconcelos and Kim (2020a, 2020b, 2022) on CS-
ModeL caught our attention. They suggest using Scratch (Resnick et al., 2009), a popular
programming platform for primary and lower secondary school. Scratch is a block-based,
agent-based, and visual-based programming language, characteristics which Vasconce-
los and Kim (2020a, 2020b) argue are beneficial when teaching the scientific practice of
modeling in science education. We therefore wanted to use their idea of modeling natural-
science phenomena by block-based programming in Scratch to promote the PSTs’ develop-
ment of TK and CK. We wanted the PSTs to encounter two kinds of simulations, repre-
senting stochastic and dynamic phenomena, to promote their knowledge of simulations in
science (i.e., TCK). We therefore chose a simulation of the moon phases and a simulation
of radioactive decay for the PSTs to work with.
Vasconcelos and Kim (2020b) provided PSTs with nearly finished code which they were
supposed to complete by entering key variables into the simulation. Rachmatullah and
Wiebe (2023), on the other hand, based their design on the UMC approach by Lee et al.
(2011), where students start with a basic, but fully functioning code. However, we wanted
to support the PSTs more explicitly in programming and instead chose the PRIMM (Sent-
ance et al., 2019) approach. To scaffold the programming in the modify-stage we devel-
oped coding cards, which are cards with small programming tasks (Lin et al., 2012). PSTs
could for example be tasked with modifying the code so that the moon has the same side
towards the earth as it rotates around the earth. This also provided PSTs with examples on
how programming could be taught to pupils in science education.
In our design, we emphasized the make-stage, where the PSTs developed their own sim-
ulation and a suggestion for a lesson plan that used the simulation they had created. This
was inspired by the idea of using learning-by-design to develop PSTs’ TPACK (Mishra &
Koehler, 2006), and also Vasconcelos and Kim (2020b) who asked the PSTs to design a
scientific modeling lesson. The difference between learning-by-design and our use of the
PRIMM-approach is the extra support intended to reduce the cognitive load.
Results from analysis of Prototype 1
All the data from Prototype 1 was analyzed to see which components of TPACK were
used by the PSTs in the learning sequence (RQ1). Results showed that much of the PSTs’
focus during programming was on TK, in the form of the technicalities of getting the
code to work, for example through tinkering or modifying the esthetics of the animation.

Quantitative analyses of the pre-post data were used to see which components of the
PSTs’ TPACK changed during the learning sequence (RQ2). The results (see Table 4) indi-
cate that PSTs’ pre-values show relatively high self-reported TK and PCK, but that TPACK
is somewhat lower. There are also rather large standard deviations in TK and TPACK in
the pre-values, indicating relatively large differences between the PSTs initially. However,
these standard deviations decrease in the post results. The pre-post differences suggest
there is an increase in the PSTs’ self-reported TK, PCK and TPACK, as all mean differ-
ences are significantly different from zero, except TK, which, however, is close to signifi-
cant (p ≈ 0.10).
Results of the fixed effects analyses in Table 5 show the change in TPACK when we
control for PSTs’ TK and PCK. The results indicate that the PSTs on average experienced
a change in TPACK of about 0.6 points, and the average individual change in TPACK is
significantly different from zero.
The regression coefficients (TK and PCK) in Table 5 show that PCK does not sig-
nificantly contribute to explain the variation in TPACK. However, it is still possible that
PCK did, as the effect size (i.e. regression coefficient) of PCK is comparable to TK. Thus,

TPACK by integrating it with their TK. However, the within-between model shown in
Table 6 suggests that the individual change in PSTs’ PCK and the differences between
PSTs’ TK are a large part of the explanation for the change in PSTs’ TPACK. This result
could be interpreted as supporting Path 3 (Koehler et al., 2014) where PSTs develop their
PCK and TPACK in concert. The quantitative analyses suggest that the latter interpretation
is more accurate. This result suggests that the PSTs develop their PCK (and CK) through
working with programming, something which has also been indicated in previous research
(Adler & Kim, 2018; Jaipal-Jamani & Angeli, 2017; Tsai et al., 2022; Vasconcelos & Kim,
2020b). A possible explanation for the low but significant increase in PCK in Prototype 1,
could be that the PSTs were allowed sufficient time in-class to develop their simulations
and lesson plans, which could have allowed them enough time to develop both PCK and
TPACK simultaneously.
Prototype 2
Problem description and revised goals
We found that the major problems to address were related to the PSTs focusing too much
on TK and too little on CK and TCK during the predict-, run-, investigate- and modify-
stages. We wanted the PSTs to use programming to learn more about the science content
and see programming as part of the scientific practice of modeling (Peel et al., 2021; Wein-
trop et al., 2016). Therefore, we would prefer the PSTs to use the simulations for scientific
inquiry. The new goals for the prototype, with amendments given in italics, were thus:
1. PSTs should develop their TPACK related to programming simulations in science.
2. PSTs should develop their TK related to programming, but programming should be
used to support the learning of science, and the programming itself should not be their
primary focus.
3. PSTs should develop CK and TCK related to scientific practices and simulations, espe-
cially by modeling and using simulations for inquiry.
Design changes
Based on our experiences, analysis of data from Prototype 1, and further reading of the
literature connected to modeling (e.g., Gouvea & Passmore, 2017; Schwarz et al., 2009;
Windschitl et al., 2008), we revised the design to shift the focus of the PSTs from strug-
gling and tinkering with the code (TK) towards science and model-based inquiry using the
simulations. To reduce the focus of the PSTs from practicing solely TK, we changed our
pedagogical approach from PRIMM, which divides the use-stage into the three steps of
predict-run-investigate (Sentance et al., 2019), to UMC (Lee et al., 2011) which has a less
elaborate use-stage.
In the use-stage we emphasized using the simulation for inquiry. This was intended to
increase the PSTs’ understanding of how simulations could be used in science (TCK). To
enhance the inquiry aspect and the CK and TCK learning, we introduced gliders in Scratch
to vary parameters. In this way, experimenting with the program became more accessi-
ble, as the PSTs did not have to edit the code and the parameters to vary were presented
visually.

text:
N. Karlsen, S. Aalbergsjø
We also replaced one of the simulations used in Prototype 1 which the PSTs found
too complex. The simulation we removed used a geometrical model to explain the moon
phases. This was replaced by a simulation based on Newtons’ laws of motion developed
for middle grade students by Aksit and Wiebe (2020). An objective with this change was
to make it easier for the PSTs to examine the mechanics of the phenomenon rather than
geometry.
To further increase the focus on scientific inquiry in the modify-stage, we revised the
coding cards to focus on questions about the scientific phenomena. These questions could
be explored by extending the code representing the model of the phenomenon being simu-
lated, for example by adding air resistance to the code. This change was inspired by the idea
of Gouvea and Passmore (2017) to have an explicit phenomenon, a clear inquiry question
and an epistemic goal. Thus, the coding cards stayed closer to the phenomena by focusing
on a particular aspect of the simulation and the scientific concepts being examined.
Results from analysis of Prototype 2
The content analysis of the video- and sound recordings from the lessons in Prototype 2
was used to investigate which components of TPACK were used by the PSTs in the learn-
ing sequence (RQ1). This showed that the PSTs still focused on TK while coding, but the
use- and modify-stages showed more CK aspects for all groups and TCK also became
prominent in these stages. While using the simulations and developing them further, the
PSTs engaged their CK when discussing the science content represented in the simulation
and the scientific mechanisms. The TCK focus became apparent when the PSTs discussed
what scientific phenomena were suitable for simulation and how to represent aspects of
these phenomena in the code.
During the create-stage, the PSTs mainly focused on TCK, while pure TK and CK were
less prominent, possibly because they had chosen to create simulations for well known sci-
ence content and applying programming elements they were comfortable with. Addition-
ally, their TPACK was visible when developing their lesson plans and discussing what type
of assignments to give to pupils. However, time constraints gave less time for the create-
stage in class, which seemed to result in more focus on TCK than TPACK during class, as
the PSTs had to finish their lesson plans later.
Quantitative analyses were used to understand which components of the PSTs’ TPACK
changed during the Prototype 2 learning sequence (RQ2). The results (see Table 7) show
similar results for the PSTs’ pre-values as for Prototype 1, but the PSTs in Prototype 2
overall report lower mean values than was found in Prototype 1. The pre-post differences

design of the learning sequence or the sample being more homogeneous than Prototype 1
due to the high attrition in Prototype 2 (cf. Table 2 which shows a reduction in PSTs from

Results of the fixed effects analysis are shown in Table 8. The intercept-value shows the
change in TPACK when we control for PSTs’ TK and PCK, and indicate that the PSTs on
average experienced a change in TPACK of about 0.6 points, similar to Prototype 1.
The regression coefficients (TK and PCK) in Table 8 show that the main difference
between the two prototypes is that also PCK contributes significantly to explaining the var-
iation in TPACK for Prototype 2. This suggests that the PSTs in Prototype 2 were able to
connect their PCK better with their TPCK than in Prototype 1, perhaps due to the changes
made to the design of the learning sequence.
The qualitative and quantitative data together provide insight into the PSTs’ paths for
developing TPACK during the learning sequence (RQ3). With regard to CK, the qualita-
tive results indicate that the PSTs emphasized CK and TCK, while the quantitative results
indicate that PSTs’ PCK—which also includes items related to CK (Karlsen et al., 2025)—
did not change significantly. This difference could be due to the fact that Newton’s laws of
motion is known content for the PSTs from previous science education courses, but also
known to be difficult to understand in-depth (Atasoy & Ergin, 2017; Weber & Wilhelm,
2024). Therefore, it is not surprising that the PSTs did not express higher CK after having
struggled with this topic in class.
Similar to Prototype 1, the quantitative results indicate that the PSTs integrated their
knowledge of TK with PCK to develop TPACK during the designed learning sequence.
The Prototype 2 results suggest that both TK and PCK contributed significantly to changes
in PSTs’ TPACK. However, if we take into account that the mean PCK did not significantly
change, as shown in Table 7, this result fits Path 1 where PSTs first develop their TK and
then integrate it with their PCK to develop TPACK. However, the difference in the mean
PCK was small and almost significant (p ≈ .10), suggesting that some of the PSTs probably
developed their PCK during the learning sequence.
The results strongly suggest that all PSTs did change their TPACK. Further, the stronger
regression coefficient for TK (cf. Table 7), suggest that Path 1 for developing TPACK,
where the PSTs integrate their TK with their PCK to develop TPACK, is found more effec-

N. Karlsen, S. Aalbergsjø
not sound unreasonable, considering that Path 3 is also known to be more cognitively tax-
ing (Koehler et al., 2014).
Derived design principles
We have discussed the process of designing a learning sequence to develop PSTs’ TPACK
related to programming simulations in science education, and analyzed the development
of PSTs’ TPACK in two iterations of the design process. The PSTs in our study are at the
master’s level in science education, and have a background with PK, CK and PCK. New
elements for the PSTs were TK, TCK, TPK and TPACK. The results strongly indicate that
PSTs’ TPACK developed during the learning sequence. In Prototype 1, the PSTs’ TK was
engaged during the use- and modify-stages and their TCK and TPACK in the create-stage,
and their change in TPACK could be explained by the individual change in the PSTs’ PCK
and differences between their TK. For Prototype 2, where design changes were made to
increase emphasis on TCK, their TK, CK and TCK were engaged in the use- and modify-
stages and their TCK at the create-stage. Here, changes in TPACK were also related to
changes in TK. Thus, the results indicate that Path 1, where PSTs develop TK in the con-
text of existing CK and PCK, could be the more promising approach to develop TPACK
when the participants are unacquainted with TK or TCK.
In the following we express the implications of our research in the form of six design
principles that we believe are important to support PSTs in developing TPACK for using
programming of simulations in science teaching.
Design principle 1: Use UMC to scaffold PSTs’ learning while working with program-
able simulations in science education.
To scaffold PSTs’ TPACK development efficiently, our results indicate that TK should
be developed and connected to existing CK along the lines of Path 1. Previous studies
have investigated PSTs who completed nearly finished code (e.g., Vasconcelos & Kim,
2020b). However, to increase PSTs’ programming experience we examined both PRIMM
and UMC as alternatives. Our analysis shows that the PSTs did not discuss science when
working within the PRIMM model, as too much focus was on the programming itself. We
therefore advocate the UMC approach, which our results indicate provides a better balance
between CK and TK.
Design principle 2: Keep the initial TK-requirements low by choosing a block-based
programming platform and a simulation code which is easy to grasp for the PSTs when
using and modifying the code.
Our results suggest that apprehensible code will enable the PSTs to more readily explore
the science phenomena being simulated in the use- and modify stages and keep the PSTs’
focus on the science content, rather than the code. We saw for example that when the simu-
lation code was too complex, the PSTs mainly focused on TK-aspects while working with
the code. We suggest using a block-based coding environment, like Scratch, to keep a low
threshold.
Design principle 3: Choose computer simulations for the use-stage that contain exam-
ples of central computational elements.
The PSTs in our study are acquainted with science, but not TK, TCK and TPACK. We
therefore chose to have the PSTs engage with two different simulations to familiarize them
with different types of computational elements (movement, clones etc.) and ways of model-
ling (deterministic and stochastic processes) to increase their TK and TCK. These elements

paper_title: Karlsen2026_PSTP_ProgrammingSimulations.pdf
text:
Developing pre‑service teachers’ TPACK for programming…
were also found in the simulations created by the PSTs. Therefore, we suggest to choose
simulations in the use-stage that include computational elements that can be useful to the
PSTs when they create simulations in the create-stage. Such computational elements can
be variables, and operators such as addition or multiplication, which are rare in PST code
(Tsai et al., 2022; Umutlu, 2022).
Design principle 4: Design the simulations in the use-stage such that PSTs can explore
the science phenomenon without programming.
The largest design change between Prototype 1 and 2 was to increase the explicit focus
on simulation-based inquiry in the use-stage. The qualitative results suggested that this
may strengthen the PSTs’ focus on TCK. We did this by including gliders in Scratch to
vary parameters in the simulation. This facilitated exploring the scientific parameters of the
program without programming.
We also saw that the PSTs focused more on the science behind the model when the
simulation was based on physical laws such as Newton’s laws, rather than on a geometri-
cal 2D-model of the moon phases. This result suggests that the simulation code should
be based on natural science models to support the students in making science-based
explanations.
Design principle 5: Use coding cards to scaffold the PSTs’ programming when they
modify how the physical mechanism of the phenomena is represented in the simulation.
In the second prototype, we changed the coding-cards for the modify-stage towards
modeling-based inquiry by posing questions that required the PSTs to use programming
to explore the phenomena, thus demonstrating how programming could be used to explore
the science content (i.e., TCK). We used programming tasks to either revise the underly-
ing mechanisms or explore the PSTs’ conceptual understanding of the model, rather than
modifying the esthetics or appearance of the animation. This change was inspired by Gou-
vea and Passmore (2017) and resulted in the PSTs displaying more TCK and CK while
programming. The need to explicitly address TCK during the modify-stage was indicated
by our results and is suggested by the work of Lee et al. (2024) who added decode as an
aspect of UMC to make explicit the relation between CT and scientific practices.
Design principle 6: Challenge the PSTs to both develop a simulation and an accompa-
nying lesson plan that includes the simulation.
The create-stage was the only stage where we found evidence of the PSTs’ TPACK and
therefore appears to be essential! We adapted the create-stage based on ideas from learn-
ing-by-design (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The idea is for PSTs to develop their TPACK
by designing course materials together with a lesson plan. This type of approach has been
found fruitful before (Aalbergsjø, 2022; Vasconcelos & Kim, 2020b, 2022), and we found
in our case that the PSTs shifted their focus in the create-stage towards TCK and TPACK
while discussing appropriate tasks for the pupils (Aalbergsjø & Karlsen, 2023).
To summarize, the presented six design principles intend to support Path 1 for TPACK
development, which was found in our analysis to be the most effective path for PSTs with a
background in science education. The principles are based on promoting TK development
in the context of science, and allow the PSTs to connect new TK and TCK to their CK and
PCK. This was done by carefully choosing example simulations and tasks for the PSTs. By
choosing examples relevant for school science this also provided the PSTs with examples
on how programming could be taught to pupils in science education, and supported their
TPACK development through exemplary instruction. Even though the above design prin-
ciples are framed in a UMC setting, we believe that they can also be relevant for other situ-
ations where programmable simulations are used for science education or within a UMC
setting with other content focus than modeling and simulations.

text:
N. Karlsen, S. Aalbergsjø
Limitations and future work
Our research reports from the prototyping stage of a DBR project. Results from DBR
are grounded in specific contexts, thereby reducing their immediate generalizability. We
therefore welcome others to apply our design principles in different contexts to explore
their generalizability and suggest suitable adaptations to other settings.
One limitation of our work is our use of a single-group pre-post test with a self-
report questionnaire to measure the effect of our learning sequence. Such designs have
weaknesses when it comes to establishing causality (Shadish et al., 2002). However, this
weakness is mitigated by comparing with qualitative analyses. Also, the relatively small
sample sizes in our study may lead to lower power when attempting to detect significant
effects (Cohen, 1990).
In our qualitative analyses, we analyzed the content listings of the recordings, rather
than the full transcripts, and the quantitative results do not distinguish between the dif-
ferent UMC-stages. There could therefore be TPACK occurrences that we have not iden-
tified in our analysis, which could explain some of the contradictory results discussed
in "Results from analysis of Prototype 1" and "Results from analysis of Prototype 2"
sections. Future research could therefore look closer at how TPACK develops during
the different stages, for example by analyzing video recordings of the programming ses-
sions more thoroughly or collecting questionnaire data or written reflection logs from
the participants in-between the different stages. Also, we have not included PSTs’ XK in
our analysis. However, this knowledge can be considered highly relevant when design-
ing learning materials and creating lesson plans for pupils. However, the purpose of
this study was not to analyze every aspect of TPACK but instead to focus on making an
investigation into promising avenues for developing TPACK.

in the Undergraduate Physics Curriculum
Executive Summary
The Undergraduate Curriculum Task Force (UCTF) of the American Association of
Physics Teachers (AAPT) was established in 2013, in part, to develop
“…recommendations for coherent and relevant curricula…for different types of physics
majors.”
To be relevant, curricula must facilitate the development of skills that are useful to
physics majors in their post-baccalaureate careers. Skills necessary for using a
computer to calculate answers to physics problems, i.e., computational physics skills,
are highly valued by research, industry, and many other employment sectors.
The American Association of Physics Teachers (AAPT) has therefore developed the
recommendations outlined in this document. These recommendations build upon a
policy that the AAPT formally adopted in 2011, urging “that every physics and
astronomy department provide its majors and potential majors with appropriate
instruction in computational physics.” Because of the variance in the student audience,
the available resources, and a department’s curriculum, the manner in which these
recommendations are implemented is ultimately a local decision.
This document provides guidance and recommendations for incorporating
computational physics into undergraduate physics programs. The reasons for doing
so include the ubiquity of computation in the practice of physics, numerous
immediate educational benefits of a computational approach, and the need to prepare
physics graduates for the workplace and advanced degree programs. In order to
develop computational physics skills, students first need to have knowledge of and
experience with a variety of computational tools and fundamental computer skills.
Technical computing skills and computational physics skills can then be built on this
foundational knowledge. We briefly describe the types of computational tools that
are widely available to enable this work. We then present a list of computation-
related skills, divided into two focus areas, technical computing skills and
computational physics skills. All physics majors should develop and practice these
skills over the entire span of their degree programs, and we provide corresponding
descriptions of learning outcome recommendations, and append specific examples.
We describe different logistical ways to insert computation into the undergraduate
curriculum, the many challenges that must be overcome in order to do so, and
resources that can help instructors and departments implement these
recommendations.
We hope this document will be useful to physics department chairs, other
administrators, curriculum committees, and individual faculty members as they
assess the computational elements in their programs and seek new opportunities to
help their students become proficient in computational physics.
